correctness.rationale: Every self-inverse signed partial monomial matrix squares to its support projection; anticommutation makes these projections central, proving the invariant four-way domain partition. A single active involution has exactly signed positive/negative fixed points and signed swaps. On both-active blocks, the commuting underlying Klein-four permutation action has transitive orbit length one, two, or four. One-point orbits are impossible; two-point orbits require exactly one generator swap and have four labeled sign assignments per type; four-point regular orbits have six labeled unsigned actions and eight sign assignments each. Their exponential component weights are 1, two copies of (2z+z²), 4z² and 2z⁴. Direct matrix census n=0..5 agrees in every coefficient. All-n proof is combinatorial, not census extrapolation.

originality.rationale: Direct comparisons with full-text literature on inverse-monoid monogenic enumeration, commuting symmetric inverse semigroups, and rook-monoid signed representations do not identify an exact anticommuting signed partial-involution block classification or joint rank exponential series. The closest prior general result on commuting finite-power partial bijections concerns unsigned commuting maps and does not imply the signed Clifford-type anticommutator obstruction. Exact-formula and alias searches found no directly equivalent statement. General monomial Clifford classifications remain a nontrivial publication-priority risk.

value.rationale: The exact full joint support-rank enumerator is a natural invariant of signed rook inverse monoids, determining all anticommuting involution pairs rather than a small numerical bound. The signed Clifford-type obstruction genuinely changes which permutation transitive blocks are allowed, yielding a sharp even-dimensional condition on the common support and an explicit 2-/4-block classification valid for all sizes. This provides a complete structural finite family result distinct from classical unsigned commutation enumeration.
